html:
The voyage of HMS Bounty, under Lieutenant William Bligh, to collect breadfruit plants in Tahiti and carry them to British plantations in the Caribbean. It ended in the most famous mutiny in naval history, on 28 April 1789.

Planters in the West Indies wanted a cheap, filling food for the enslaved people who worked their estates. Joseph Banks, who had seen breadfruit in Tahiti with Cook, backed the plan. The Bounty left England in December 1787 and stayed five months on Tahiti while the crew potted over a thousand young trees. Three weeks after leaving, the acting lieutenant Fletcher Christian led a mutiny. Bligh and 18 loyal men were set adrift in an open boat. He sailed it some 6,700 km to Timor, one of the great feats of seamanship.

The mutineers took Tahitian men and women to remote Pitcairn Island, where their descendants still live. Bligh came back on a second voyage and in 1793 landed breadfruit in Jamaica and St Vincent. At first the enslaved workers would not eat it, but it became a staple of the islands. The voyage links Pacific plants to the Atlantic slave economy.
